analysis.one_liner: Eases environmental review for forest-thinning projects near communities and subsidizes biomass use of removed wood.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Mike Crapo with one Democratic cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let federal agencies thin forests near towns and municipal watersheds to cut wildfire risk, but would also exempt those projects from the normal requirement to study alternatives under the National Environmental Policy Act, replace the existing administrative appeals process with a narrower one, and shorten deadlines and limits for lawsuits. It would also fund grants for companies that buy wood removed in thinning, watershed assistance to states, forest research, and a program paying private landowners to restore habitat. It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Rural communities near fire-prone federal forests would gain funded work to protect homes and watersheds, with contracts directed to local businesses and youth crews. Biomass energy plants, wood-products firms, and timber operators would gain subsidies of up to $20 per green ton of biomass, value-added grants, and thinning and research projects that are harder for opponents to appeal or sue over.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural wildfire-risk towns and biomass firms

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Agriculture and Interior Departments to give priority to fuels-reduction projects that protect communities and municipal watersheds from catastrophic wildfire.
Requires public notice, a public meeting near the affected forest, and collaboration with state and local governments and Indian tribes during the preparation of each thinning project.
Establishes a watershed forestry cost-share program for communities and nonindustrial private forest landowners, covering up to 75 percent of project costs.
Authorizes local preference contracting so thinning and monitoring work goes to rural businesses, nonprofits, and youth conservation crews that hire local workers.

Creates a Healthy Forests Reserve Program paying private landowners to restore forest habitat for threatened and endangered species through 10-year agreements, 30-year easements, or permanent easements.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the authorized spending, about $90 million a year across the grant, watershed, research, and reserve programs. Citizens would lose procedural leverage over federal forest work: no alternatives analysis in the environmental review, a narrower appeals process open only to prior commenters, a 15-day window to file a lawsuit, and preliminary injunctions capped at 45 days. The cost of those limits falls on anyone seeking to challenge a federal thinning or logging project, and on forest ecosystems if projects go too far.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and citizens challenging forest projects

drawbacks.text: The Secretary would not be required to study, develop, or describe any alternative to the proposed agency action in the environmental assessment or impact statement for a thinning project.
The bill would replace the existing Forest Service appeals process with a single administrative process open only to people who submitted written comments during project preparation.

Lawsuits challenging a thinning project would have to be filed within 15 days of notice of final agency action, any preliminary injunction would be limited to 45 days, and courts would be pressed to reach a final ruling within 100 days.
Applied silvicultural research projects, which can include timber harvesting, thinning, and prescribed burning, would be categorically excluded from National Environmental Policy Act review.

The bill authorizes $25 million a year in grants, up to $20 per green ton, to facilities that purchase biomass for energy or products, putting public money behind a commercial demand for wood removed from public land.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wildfire risk the bill addresses is real: its own findings describe roughly 190 million acres of federal land at risk of catastrophic fire, and thinning near towns and watersheds is widely accepted as worthwhile. The bill retains basic public notice, comment, and collaboration steps, and its community-protection and watershed programs are modest and locally popular. But its most distinctive provisions are the procedural ones: skipping alternatives analysis, narrowing appeals, and cutting court deadlines serve whoever wants projects to move faster, which in practice includes operators who sell the wood removed. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill couples genuine community fire protection with a broad reduction in the public's ability to slow or stop individual federal logging projects, and that the two are hard to separate once enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on July 23, 2003 by Sen. Mike Crapo, with Sen. Blanche Lincoln joining as the bill's other introducer.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no committee report, hearing, vote, or floor action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the environmental-review exemption, the narrower appeals process, and the shortened court deadlines it contained never took effect through it, so citizens' existing avenues for commenting on and suing over federal forest projects were left intact. Biomass and timber operators went without the new purchase subsidies and easier projects, and communities near fire-prone forests did not receive the bill's new grant programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Citizens' review and lawsuit rights stayed intact

for.role: U.S. Senator from Idaho; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 23, 2003 and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was referred to committee and never moved again.

for.name: Sen. Blanche Lincoln
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arkansas; original cosponsor

for.name: Forest products and biomass industry groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported 108th Congress legislation to speed hazardous-fuels reduction on federal land and expand commercial use of removed wood, which is the policy this bill embodied in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 23, 2003 and took no further action; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Environmental and conservation organizations
against.role: Opponents of narrowed environmental review and litigation limits
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against healthy-forests legislation during the 108th Congress that would exempt forest projects from alternatives analysis and limit lawsuits and injunctions over federal thinning and logging.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded vote exists; sponsorship was nearly all Republican, with exactly one Democratic cosponsor joining the Republican sponsor, and the bill never advanced far enough to divide either chamber.

industries.note: Hazardous-fuels projects on national forests and BLM land yield merchantable trees, and this bill would make those projects harder for citizens to slow or stop: no alternatives analysis in the environmental review, a replacement appeals process open only to prior commenters, a 15-day lawsuit deadline, and injunctions capped at 45 days. The industry's gain comes from reduced public oversight of work on public land.

The bill would pay facilities up to $20 per green ton for biomass they buy, plus value-added grants, and expand biomass research funding, making them the permanent commercial outlet for wood removed in fuels-reduction work. Burning small-diameter wood can help fund real fire-risk reduction near communities, but the subsidy also gives facilities a standing financial interest in continued removal from public land at public expense.

industries.industry: Rural forest communities and small contractors
industries.note: Local preference contracting directs thinning and monitoring contracts to rural businesses, nonprofits, and youth crews, and the watershed cost-share and reserve programs send money to towns and small private landowners. These provisions align with the interests of people living in fire-prone areas.
